sections.html:
Ouachita Parish is in northern Louisiana. Monroe is the seat and largest municipality, and West Monroe sits across the Ouachita River from it. They are the parish's only two cities, and Richwood and Sterlington are its towns. The 2020 census counted 160,368 people, and the 2025 estimate is 158,542. Unincorporated communities that show up on property records include Bawcomville, Brownsville, Calhoun, Claiborne, Lakeshore and Swartz.

Housing here comes from several growth waves, starting with the natural gas boom that began in 1916 and drew workers in the 1920s. Whatever decade your house dates from, expect buyers to ask about the age of the roof, wiring and plumbing. Schools depend on the address: the Monroe City School System serves areas within Monroe and the Ouachita Parish School Board runs public schools elsewhere, so check before describing schools to a buyer.

The Assessor values property and the Sheriff collects the tax. The Louisiana Constitution and Legislature set the framework, and the Louisiana Tax Commission writes the assessment rules. Local bodies such as the police jury and school board set the levies that appear on a bill.

OfficeWhat it doesHow to reach it
Ouachita Parish AssessorLists and values all taxable property, tracks homestead exemptionsRecords searchable online
Ouachita Parish Sheriff, Civil/Tax OfficeEx-officio tax collector(318) 324-2536; pay by mail, in person or online
Board of ReviewFirst appeal step after the AssessorAsk the Assessor for dates
Louisiana Tax CommissionSecond appeal stepState agency

The Assessor's site at opassessor.com has a property search, an interactive map, millage rates by ward and a tax calculator. The Sheriff posts tax information at opso.net.

The Assessor takes fair market value and applies a statutory percentage. Land and residential improvements are assessed at 10 percent of fair market value. Commercial property, including personal property, is at 15 percent, though commercial land is at 10 percent.

The $7,500 maximum homestead exemption comes off the assessed value before the millage is applied. It does not reduce city taxes, so a house inside Monroe or West Monroe can carry a higher total bill than one outside them.

Louisiana requires reassessment at least every four years, and a property can be reassessed any time after a sale or a change. The Assessor also asks new buyers to complete a Sales Questionnaire, which helps check fair market value.

Louisiana's general rule is that bills go out in December and taxes are due December 31, with interest of 1 percent per month on late balances. The Sheriff's Tax Office takes payments by mail, in person or online.

A missing notice does not excuse payment. If no bill came, ask the tax collector what is owed.

  • Bills are mailed once a year, in December.
  • Late balances accrue interest at 1 percent a month.
  • Unpaid property can go to a tax sale, and a debtor has three years to redeem immovable property sold that way.
  • Foreclosure and seizure sales run through the Sheriff's Civil Division, with auctions on Wednesday mornings at 10 a.m. through an online platform.

Talk to the Assessor first. If you still disagree, appeal to the Ouachita Parish Board of Review, then to the Louisiana Tax Commission, and finally to the courts.

Bring evidence that the valuation is wrong. Recent sale prices, an appraisal and photographs of damage are the kinds of material Louisiana boards accept. Outside Orleans Parish, the public can inspect the tax roll between August 15 and September 15. Missing the appeal window usually means waiting for the next tax year.

sections.h2: Homestead exemption and the age freeze
sections.html:
The main reductions are the homestead exemption and the special assessment freeze for older owners. The homestead exemption is $7,500 of assessed value, which equals $75,000 of market value, for an owner-occupied home, and it can cover up to 160 acres that include an owner-occupied residence.

The Assessor's website links to an application postcard and a page about the Special Assessment Value Freeze for owners 65 and older. The freeze can also apply to owners with a service-connected disability of at least 50 percent, subject to an income limit. The Assessor also publishes a veterans brochure. Both benefits follow the person living in the home, so a buyer applies separately.

Unpaid taxes are a lien on the property and must be cleared for clean title to pass. Under La. R.S. 47:1993, once the assessment roll is delivered to the recorder of mortgages, it acts as a lien and privilege on each assessed property and generally ranks ahead of other encumbrances.

The closing attorney or title company asks the Sheriff's Tax Office for a payoff and pays it from your proceeds. Deeds are recorded with the Ouachita Parish Clerk of Court on South Grand Street in Monroe. If the house also carries a mortgage, back taxes and repairs, the title work can take longer, so start the payoff request early.

  1. Search your parcel on the Assessor's site and confirm the owner and homestead status.
  2. Call the Tax Office at (318) 324-2536 for the balance.
  3. Give the title company the payoff figure and any survey.
  4. At closing, the balance comes out of the proceeds and the deed goes to the clerk.

Errors found in step one are easier to fix before a buyer's attorney finds them.

faqs.q: When are Ouachita Parish property taxes due?
faqs.a: The general Louisiana rule is December 31, and late balances accrue 1 percent interest per month. Call the Sheriff's Tax Office at (318) 324-2536 to confirm the deadline for your bill.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Ouachita Parish?
faqs.a: The Ouachita Parish Sheriff, acting as ex-officio tax collector. You can pay by mail, in person or online through the Sheriff's website.

faqs.q: What is the Ouachita Parish homestead exemption?
faqs.a: It is $7,500 of assessed value, equal to $75,000 of fair market value, on an owner-occupied home. It does not apply to city taxes.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Ouachita Parish assessment?
faqs.a: Meet with the Assessor, then appeal to the Ouachita Parish Board of Review, then to the Louisiana Tax Commission.

faqs.q: Do I owe property tax at closing in Ouachita Parish?
faqs.a: Unpaid taxes are a lien and must be cleared for clear title, so the balance is normally paid from the sale proceeds. Your closing attorney or title company requests the figure from the Tax Office.
